title: One Million Feet Of Climbing In 2026: Third-Quarter Update – Travis Engel
content:
Travis is now in the home stretch of his attempt to log a million feet of climbing in 2026. He’s gotten through the hottest months of the summer, as well as a weeks-long content-producing cram-session to make room for a trip to Europe. But he had a setback between the months of August and September, and between vertebrae T-12 and L-2.

Photo: Brian Vernor

It’s not looking good, folks. Three months ago, my quest to climb a million feet in 2026 was in a real “trust-the-struggle” stage. I had been consistently behind schedule by 10,000 to 15,000 feet since late spring. But that proved to be an oddly educational experience. It wasn’t fun being in a rut, even an imaginary rut on my way to an arbitrary goal. It had an antimotivational effect. Thankfully, a ten to fifteen K debt is not insurmountable. And by mid August, I was back on track. That shifted my reinforcement from negative to positive, and the future was bright. Then, something happened.

Like most people entering their late 40s, I have back problems. And like most people with back problems, I’m best at physical therapy when the pain is at its worst. I had slacked off my stretches during six months of quiet comfort. That quiet was suddenly shattered when I apparently had a careless posture and / or an underinflated sleeping pad during a chainsaw mission / campout on August 22nd / 23rd. I barely made it back to the car. My back was frozen for the next two days, and my neck soon followed.

No worries, though. This has happened before, and I have a handful of simple exercises to fix it. That’s fortunate, because less than a month later, I would be leaving for Europe to hang with family and then embark on an 800-mile ride from Switzerland to Spain. A little last hurrah on the CheckOUT full-suspension gravel bike before I finally send it back to Trek.

Spoiler alert: I didn’t finish the ride. My physical therapy did eventually get me back into pedaling shape, but then came a week-long wall of unrelenting rain across most of western Europe. I was at a train station and on hold with Virgin Atlantic Airlines before you could say, “Je ne parle pas français.” But that’s another story.

Back in August, my excitement around this trip was utterly intoxicating. Maintaining my lead on the million-foot mission took a distant back seat to the more urgent task of rest and rehabilitation. Riding was painful, so I stayed off the bike for a week. Then another week, and another still. And to my surprise, I couldn’t care less that my goal was slipping away at the rate of 2,739.73 feet per day. In fact, as I write this paragraph, I still haven’t checked to see how far behind I am. Let’s do that now…

Wow. I’m about 70,000 feet behind. That’s almost three times the deficit I had at my lowest point this year. And since I’m currently in the middle of a pretty brutal heat wave here in Los Angeles, I’m not that motivated to start catching for a few more days. By then, the gap will have grown to 80K. But I think I’ve made peace with it.

Even though that Europe ride only lasted for five days, those days were devoid of pain and full of pleasure. I ate some great food, bagged some gorgeous peaks, and got woken up in the middle of the night by a wild French boar. I even took a detour to visit the H.R. Giver museum, which I had wanted to visit since I was 17.

During the preceding month, the pain was too severe and too acute to ride through. But had I tried, none of these things may have happened. My attempt to bag a million feet of climbing has taught me a lot of lessons, and this latest one was to keep my priorities straight. To not be too precious about things that don’t really matter. In the future, I feel like I’ll be better equipped to let go. And anyway, I’m pretty proud of what I’ve achieved so far.

Until just before my back started acting up in August, the most climbing I’d ever recorded in a year was 672,355 feet. I’m now at 691,782. So, every foot I climb is setting a new record. It’s like Samwise Gamgee stopping in the cornfield to say that, if he took one more step, it’d be the farthest from home he’d ever been. I know that scene isn’t anywhere in the books, but it’s a character-accurate contemplation on the struggle between comfort and growth. Between probable safety and potential failure. More than ever, failure feels very likely. But I’ve got some of the best months of the year ahead of me. Anything can happen. And more importantly, it doesn’t really matter.
